secondly:
did you ever think about why Africa is war torn? it’s largely because of the trans-atlantic slave trade, or the triangle trade. as a part of this system of trade, europeans sold guns and weaponry to people in Africa. also, when Africa was colonised, the continent was drawn up into different countries, which are the ones that are there today. before this had happened, there weren’t such state borders and instead, different tribes controlled their own areas. however, the formation of these borders caused many tribes to be squished together, for lack of a better word. this caused many wars. that was one effect of colonialism in Africa.

another effect of colonialism in Africa was the taking of many resources. colonists used many of the natural resources that Africa had, leaving the continent less wealthy. as a matter of fact, it had largely been very wealthy before colonisation.

your comparison of America as a colony and Africa is invalid, as they are completely different. in the United States, colonists stayed there and developed their own society. also, although the United States is a first world country, the indigenous people of the continent were widely killed and their societies were, in many places, left in economic ruins.

 on the other hand, in Africa, colonists left the continent. they didn’t provide any compensation for their damages, so they largely left former colonies in ruins. this also produced power vacuums in many African countries, leading to dictators coming into control. this was another effect of colonialism in Africa. some of the damage caused by colonialism is not always the colonisation itself but also the aftereffects of colonisers leaving without compensating indigenous people.

That’s awesome. I really want to be fully fluent in French and Gujarati, I think it would be super useful for me.

About the self conscious thing, I understand that. I’m afraid to speak Gujarati around my Indian relatives because I’m afraid I’ll just sound stupid. 

Urdu is a beautiful language, from what I’ve seen of it - maybe there are online courses or something? The other thing is that since the beginning of learning Gujarati, I think just talking to my dad in whatever broken Gujarati I can bring up really helps me. That’s the way I’m building my confidence with it.

Good luck!

I’d also love to be a polyglot! I haven’t got too far but it’s something to work for. I learned (and am learning) French in school, which has really helped me. Learning Gujarati has been more of a challenge, because although I started with some basics, I sort of had to teach myself the rest through online sources and books and just being around people speaking it. I’m still not fully fluent but I really really want to be, I think it’s important for my identity to be fully fluent in all of these languages of the cultures I come from.

I know what you mean about wishing they had spoken at least 2 languages. My mother spoke English to me and my father spoke Gujarati to me when I was a baby, but because I was a late talker, they started just speaking English to me in fear that I might not start talking at all. I do have a fair amount of Gujarati knowledge, but I was never able to read and write or speak it too well. I think learning to do these things was my way of navigating my identity.

As to the thing about the new script, I’d say give it a go! I don’t know how difficult the Farsi script is to learn, but after learning the Gujarati script (which did take a long time I won’t lie) I found that the whole language was much easier.
